Name: Ken Saladin
Question: How is it determined that receptor-mediated endocytosis occurs in cells? Can you provide some examples of this process occurring in humans?
Answer: In some cases, it can be observed by electron microscopy showing an environmental ligand (the molecule that binds to the receptor) being bound and taken into the cell. This is a series of photos and interpretive drawings of this from my Anatomy & Physiology textbook. I don’t know anything about the technique for visualizing this—for example, whether some sort of label has to be bound to ligand molecules before one can introduce them to living cells and observe this. Osmium tetroxide is commonly used to stain cells for transmission electon microscopy; maybe that’s all this is. Some examples are that this is how endothelial cells (the walls of blood capillaries) take up low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) from the blood; how they take up insulin to be transported from the bloodstream, across the capillary wall, to the surrounding tissues such as liver and muscle; and it’s how hepatitis, polio, and HIV (AIDS viruses) are taken up and estabilsh infections in the body by “tricking” the endothelial cells into binding and transporting them.

Question: What do most retired people over 70 do all day?
Answer: I’m halfway through my 70s now, and have been retired from teaching for 7 years. What do I do with my days? Well…. Each morning over coffee and breakfast, I share knbowledge and opinions on Quora, keep in touch with friends in Faebook, work New York Times puzzles (crosswords, Sudoku, etc.), entertain my cats, and whatever else pops up. Every Monday I go to a deli for coffee and brunch with friends, and every Friday I go to lunch with a neuroscientist who filled my faculty position when I retired. Evenings, I watch the broadcast news and Jeopardy!, and some days, a few favorite shows (mostly BBC) my wife and I like. She likes more TV shows than I do, so I’m more inclined to pass the evenings reading, and usually have at least two or three books going at once. I publish a scientific textbook almost every January, raning about 780 to 1200 pages with hundred of color illustrations. I’m always keeping up with literature and working on updates and improvements in these books. When book production is in certain stages, I work about 4–5 hours a day writing and illustrating them, and sometimes work up to 10 hours a day when there’s a lot to be done on a tight schedule. I work with production teams in the US and India, and I’m mentoring younger coauthors who will be my successors when I decide to get out of publishing. I expect to actively author books until I’m 85 or so. I have a small house but large land, and I’m outdoors almost every day taking care of the property in one way or another. This week, chainsawing and removing four storm-fallen trees, doing 2–3 hours of mowing, and sodding a bare area. I travel to professional conferences to keep up with my colleagues and advances in my professional field; travel to visit my adult children and grandson; and take my wife on travel vacations (a European river cruise not long ago; fall colors at an Appalachian mountain lodge coming up; and driving the Ring Road around Iceland coming up a little later). And I have ample lazy do-nothing hours also. It’s a full enough life.
